qrdBas-b1102z-d1e101.summary: Fragmentary opening (the preceding folios 167v-168r are missing from the witness). The surviving words, '...its willing, and which is in the power of the will', end a sentence about thought (cogitatio) as something within the will's power, the topic of the following replies.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e117.summary: Specifies what cognition must precede the will's command over a thought. Habitual cognition of the act does not suffice, nor universal cognition (as actual cognition of 'animal' does not suffice for a distinct volition of man or ass). The thought must be known in some way distinctly and in particular on the side of the object (this thought about this object), even if imperfectly on the knower's side; otherwise the will would cause the thought by chance.
claims: Neither habitual nor universal cognition suffices for the will to command a thought.
The commanded thought must be known with some particular distinctness on the side of the object.
Without such cognition, the will would cause the thought by chance.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e146.summary: Raises the follow-up question: what causes the first thought that precedes the will's act regarding thinking?

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e151.summary: Answers that, on this approach, the first thought is caused only by the object that moves most strongly, in its own phantasm or another's. Even if habitual knowledge sufficed, the question would remain which object, together with the will, causes the first thought that lies in the will's power. The sentence breaks off and continues into the next paragraph.
claims: The first thought is caused by the most strongly moving object via phantasms.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e170.summary: Concludes that thought is in the will's power, so venial or even mortal sin can occur in thought, as in lingering delectation on something illicit that should have been rejected (morose delectation, per Augustine). Sin lies principally in the will's delight in an illicit object and its holding the intellect on it, so interior sin of will and thought differs from sins of word and deed. The object must be willed at least interpretatively; delight in the knowability of evil is not sin, as Augustine's grammarian enjoys knowing a solecism without committing one ('to know evil is not evil, to will evil is'). Then begins replies to others' objections. Thought can be caused not only by memory but by the concurring will, which has per se partial causality in producing the word (verbum), so the word comes freely on the will's side and naturally on memory's, like creatures' effects, which are free from the divine will (a total cause) and natural from natural causes.
claims: Thought is in the power of the will, so sin can occur in thought alone.
Morose delectation in an illicit object can be mortal sin.
Interior sin consists principally in the will's delight and its holding the intellect on the illicit object.
Delight in knowing evil as knowable is not sin.
The will is a per se partial cause of the mental word, which is thus produced freely and naturally under different respects.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e244.summary: Reply to a second objection (that the commanded thought must precede the will's act): the thought in the will's power is posterior in nature and in real effect to the will's act about it, yet prior in concept through another thought about it. A willed or known object need not be prior in itself; it suffices that it be prior in something representing it or moving to knowledge of it.
claims: The commanded thought is really posterior to the volition but conceptually prior via another thought.
An object can be prior to a volition through its representation rather than in itself.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e262.summary: Reply to a third objection (circular causation): there is no circle among per se causes, at least in the same genus. The posterior thought is not a real cause of the volition; rather a previous thought about the future thought is, and thus a non-existent object is a partial cause of the volition not in itself but in its representation, if the object is a partial cause at all.
claims: There is no circularity among per se causes in the same genus.
A non-existent object causes volition only through its representation in a prior act of understanding.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e286.summary: Reply to a fourth objection: the will is a partial agent of such an act, so other causes, however close, do not suffice unless the will acts or co-causes.
claims: The will is a necessary partial co-cause of the commanded thought.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e295.summary: Reply to a fifth objection (that a thought, being an act and not an object, cannot be in the will's power): a thought does not differ by the nature of the thing in being object and act. The same thing is both, and as such can be posited in reality and be preceded in concept by another act about it.
claims: One and the same thought is both act and object without real distinction.
A thought can be posited in reality by the will and anticipated by another act.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e313.summary: Reply to a sixth objection: there is no problem with two thoughts (one about the other) coexisting in the intellect, as with direct and reflex acts. Then treats speech and exterior deed: they are in the will's power insofar as the will freely moves or commands the organs. Sin is in speech not essentially (speech being a quality in the air distinct from the speaker) but in its causation through the organs. It is sinful when ordered against its imposed end of expressing the mind's concept, as in deceiving, or when expressing a concept improperly (harmfully or idly). A deed is sinful when it falls short of the perfection right reason requires. Ends the second article.
claims: Direct and reflex thoughts can coexist in the intellect.
Speech and deed are in the will's power through its command of the bodily organs.
Sin in speech lies in its causation and its ordering against its proper end of expressing the mind's concept.
Sin in deed is a failure of the perfection required by right reason.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e353.summary: Begins the third article: sin is divided in five ways. First, by effects: venial sin does not deprive of grace and eternal life and merits temporal punishment; mortal sin deprives of grace and eternal life and merits eternal punishment.
claims: Mortal sin deprives of grace and eternal life and merits eternal punishment; venial sin merits only temporal punishment.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e371.summary: Second division, by roots, from Augustine on the Psalm ('incensa igni et suffosa'): sin from love that wrongly inflames ('burnt with fire') and sin from fear that wrongly humbles ('dug down').
claims: Sins arise from disordered love or from disordered fear.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e384.summary: Third division, by branches: sins of thought, speech, and deed.
claims: Sin is divided into thought, word, and deed.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e391.summary: Fourth division, by objects: sin against God, against oneself, and against one's neighbor.
claims: Sin is divided by its object into sins against God, self, and neighbor.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e398.summary: Fifth division, by precepts and prohibitions (from Augustine's Questions on Leviticus): sin of omission (not doing what is commanded) and of commission (doing what is forbidden). For brevity the author passes over the Master's sevenfold division of mortal (capital) sins. Ends the third article.
claims: Sins are divided into omission and commission.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e414.summary: Reply to the first principal argument (of the question on interior and exterior sin): an exterior act and its corresponding interior act are one only by order; they need not share one indivisible goodness or malice, since one is good or bad through the other.
claims: Interior and exterior acts form a unity of order, not a single indivisible goodness or malice.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e431.summary: Reply to the second principal argument: willing to fornicate and fornicating are formally two sins, yet interior and exterior acts are ordered to one principle, the will that elicits the interior act and commands the exterior one, and concern the same matter. At the page break to folio 169r the text shifts abruptly to the sin against the Holy Spirit, which is perhaps called 'irremissible' de facto because it is never, or only rarely, forgiven. The discontinuity suggests further missing or displaced text in the witness.
claims: Willing a sinful deed and doing it are formally two sins ordered to one principle.
The sin against the Holy Spirit is called irremissible because in fact it is never or rarely forgiven.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e455.summary: Heading announcing the third article (of the question on the power of sinning).

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e462.summary: First point of the article: whether the power of sinning is from God.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e467.summary: Second point of the article: whether the power of sinning belongs intrinsically to free choice (liberum arbitrium).

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e472.summary: First argument that the power of sinning is not from God: an equivocal cause contains its effect eminently, so God would have the power of sinning.
claims: An equivocal cause has its effect eminently, so God would have the power of sinning.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e481.summary: Second argument: as the act, so the power; the act of sinning is evil, so the power is evil, and evil is not from God.
claims: The power takes its character from its act, so the power of sinning would be evil.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e489.summary: Third argument: in the power of sinning the creature is not likened to God, so it is not from God.
claims: The power of sinning involves no likeness to God.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e494.summary: Fourth argument: the power of sinning is just the will to sin, and the will to sin is no more from God than sin is.
claims: The power of sinning is the will to sin, which is not from God.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e503.summary: The author announces his own answer, which proceeds by distinguishing senses of 'power'.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e510.summary: First sense of 'power': the principle by which something acts or is acted upon.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e517.summary: Second sense: the order or relation to the act grounded in such a principle. In the first sense the power of sinning is the created will. In the second sense, before the act exists the relation is nothing real in act; it is either a relation of reason or a merely potential relation, which becomes a real relation to a real positive act once the act exists. This holds for sins of commission, not omission, where there is no act.
claims: In the first sense the power of sinning is the created will itself.
Before the sinful act, the relation to it is only of reason or merely potential.
Once a sin of commission is posited, a real relation to the real positive act exists; in omission there is no such act.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e543.summary: Applies the first sense: the power of sinning, being the created will, must be from God like every positive reality. The will is created with and is consubstantial with the soul or spirit, which is had only by creation.
claims: The power of sinning, taken as the will, is from God like every positive reality.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e557.summary: Applies the sense of 'power' as a relation of reason to the act (called here the 'third mode'): nothing prevents God from making such a relation by his intellect comparing the power to the future act, as our intellect can too. But the divine relation is eternal and ours temporal, so they are not the same. The same holds for the relation of reason to omission, whether to something positive or to the privation of due rectitude.
claims: God can cause a relation of reason between the power and the act by his intellect's comparison.
God's comparing relation is eternal and ours temporal, so they differ.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e590.summary: Applies the sense of 'power' as a real positive relation to the act once the act exists: it too must be from God, like every positive being in act.
claims: The real relation of power to an actual sinful act is from God like every positive being.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e601.summary: Before the act exists, such a relation exists only in potency and is not from God as an actual efficient cause, but only as something not repugnant to being caused by God.
claims: A merely potential relation is not actually caused by God, though it can be caused by him.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e612.summary: Reply to the first argument: taking the power of sinning for what is positively real in it, God has it supereminently, as he has running or the power to run eminently without being able to run. The relation of reason implied by 'power' in some sense need not be in God eminently.
claims: God contains the positive reality of the power of sinning supereminently without being able to sin.
Relations of reason need not be eminently contained in God.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e634.summary: Reply to the second argument: the sinful act is good in its positive reality, and so is the power to it; God causes both but not their malice or deformity. Alternatively, an evil act does not require an evil subjective power, since good is the subject of evil.
claims: The positive reality of the sinful act and its power is good and caused by God.
God does not cause the deformity of sin.
Good is the subject of evil.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e652.summary: Reply to the fourth argument (first part): 'will to sin' can mean the act of willing to sin, as Augustine and Anselm often use 'voluntas'; in that sense the power of sinning is not the will, since a power is not its act. God causes what is positive in such willing but is neither the efficient nor the 'deficient' cause of its deformity.
claims: 'Will' can mean the act of willing, which is not the power.
God causes the positive in sinful volition, but is neither efficient nor deficient cause of its deformity.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e669.summary: Reply to the fourth argument (second part): taking 'will' as the power, the will to sin, or power of sinning, is not sin but something good in its positive reality, of which God is per se cause; evil is caused by good.
claims: The power of sinning is not itself sin but a good of which God is per se cause.
Evil is caused by good.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e682.summary: Reply to the third argument: the power of sinning, which is the created will, belongs to the image of the Trinity in the creature, so the creature is partially likened to God in its positive reality.
claims: The created will, as the power of sinning, belongs to the image of the Trinity and likens the creature to God.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e693.summary: Opens the second point with a first opinion: the power of sinning does not belong intrinsically to free choice, since free choice is in God and the blessed, who cannot sin; the power of sinning is not a pure perfection; and Anselm (De libertate arbitrii) says the ability to sin is neither liberty nor part of it.
claims: Free choice exists in God and the blessed without the power to sin.
The power of sinning is not a pure perfection.
Per Anselm, the ability to sin is no part of freedom.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e713.summary: Second opinion: although the power of sinning is not in the notion of free choice taken universally, it is intrinsic to created free choice. Reasons: it alone distinguishes created, defective free choice from the divine; God cannot make a creature naturally impeccable; and the power of sinning is also the power of not sinning, hence a power for opposites, a rational power, and rational powers belong to free choice.
claims: The power of sinning is intrinsic to created, though not to universal, free choice.
It distinguishes created from divine free choice.
God cannot make a naturally impeccable creature.
The power of sinning is a rational power for opposites.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e742.summary: The author's own third way, first member: if the power of sinning means the principle eliciting the sinful act, it is the will, the first and principal such principle in the creature. In that sense it is the whole of free choice or intrinsic to it, since the will alone is the free principle in the creature.
claims: Taken as the eliciting principle, the power of sinning is the will.
The will alone is the free principle in creatures, so in this sense it is intrinsic to free choice.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e764.summary: Second member: if 'power of sinning' means any relation grounded in that principle to a positive or privative act, it does not belong intrinsically or essentially to free choice, created or uncreated. Free choice is something positive and absolute. A real relation is sometimes only potential while free choice is actual. No ens rationis belongs to the essence of a real being. And with such relations removed, free choice would remain.
claims: The power of sinning taken as a relation is not intrinsic to any free choice.
Free choice is something absolute and positive.
No relation of reason belongs to the essence of a real being.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e798.summary: Qualifies the account: these relations necessarily accompany, in act or potency, the created will, which is the power of sinning and the same as peccable free choice. Free choice simply and in common abstracts from the power of sinning, since God has perfect free choice without it. Created free choice, however, does not, because its nature is created and free and its liberty imperfect, able to act rightly or not; it has this from its own positive nature, just as God from his uncreated nature cannot sin.
claims: The relations to sinning necessarily accompany the created will.
Free choice in common abstracts from the power to sin; created free choice does not.
Created freedom's peccability flows from its own positive nature, as God's impeccability flows from his.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e829.summary: Transitional remark: the replies to the others' arguments follow from the foregoing.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e834.summary: Reply to the first opinion's first argument: the power of sinning does not belong to free choice simply and in common, since it is not in God, but the power of sinning that is the will belongs to created free choice. The blessed do have the power of sinning, as they have a will, but it is never reduced to act, and so they are called impeccable. How and why will appear in Book IV.
claims: The blessed retain the power of sinning but it is never actualized.
The power of sinning belongs to created, not universal, free choice.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e860.summary: Reply to the second argument: the power of sinning taken as the will is a pure perfection and so belongs to (at least created) free choice; taken as the accompanying relations it is not a pure perfection and is not intrinsic. Alternatively, it is not intrinsic to free choice taken universally.
claims: As the will, the power of sinning is a pure perfection; as the accompanying relations, it is not.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e878.summary: Reply to the Anselm argument: answered by the same distinction.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e883.summary: Reply to the second opinion's first reason: it is true that created free choice is distinguished from uncreated by the power of sinning, if that means the created will itself, but not by the accompanying relations, which do not primarily distinguish them.
claims: Created free choice differs from uncreated by the created will itself, not by its relations to sinning.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e904.summary: Reply to the second reason: created free choice cannot be separated from the created will, any more than from itself. Though it cannot be separated from the relations (at least in potency), they do not belong intrinsically to it.
claims: Inseparability does not imply intrinsic belonging.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e917.summary: Reply to the third reason: the power of sinning (the will itself) and the power of not sinning belong to free choice as a rational power, though perhaps not every rational power is essentially intrinsic to free choice. Concludes the question.
claims: The will, as a rational power for sinning and not sinning, belongs to free choice.
Not every rational power need be essentially intrinsic to free choice.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e935.summary: Reply to the first principal argument (of the question on the sin against the Holy Spirit): that sin is irremissible in the sense explained earlier.
claims: The sin against the Holy Spirit is irremissible in a qualified sense.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e944.summary: Against the claim that there is no distinct sin against the Holy Spirit: there is, although every mortal sin offends the whole Trinity. It is called 'against the Spirit' not because it offends only the Spirit but for the reason given earlier.
claims: There is a distinct sin against the Holy Spirit.
Every mortal sin offends the whole Trinity.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e957.summary: Reply to the second principal argument, on obstinacy: it takes obstinacy as it is found in the damned.
claims: The argument concerns obstinacy as in the damned.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e962.summary: Reply to the third principal argument, on impossibility of remission on the part of the one forgiving or the one forgiven.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e970.summary: Reply to the fourth argument, from Christ's death: these arguments show that the sin against the Holy Spirit is not simply and absolutely irremissible, though it is irremissible in some qualified way.
claims: The sin against the Holy Spirit is not absolutely irremissible.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e983.summary: Reply to the arguments for the opposite: the Savior means not that the sin is simply irremissible, but that it is remitted only with difficulty, in this age and so in the next.
claims: Christ's saying means the sin is forgiven only with difficulty, not never.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e994.summary: Reply on the 'sin unto death' (1 John 5:16): it can be understood as final sin in which one dies, for which one should not pray by common law, except by special revelation, as Gregory prayed for the damned Trajan, who was recalled to life by God's clemency. Closes the Book II commentary with a doxology.
claims: The 'sin unto death' is final impenitence.
One should not pray for those who die in final sin, barring special revelation.
Gregory's prayer for Trajan is an exceptional case of divine clemency.

qrdBas-b1102z-d1e1012.summary: Printer's colophon closing the Book II questions: praises Bassolis, records printing in Paris at the expense of the booksellers François Regnault and Jean Frellon by the printer Nicolas des Prés, dated the last day of October 1516, with a closing motto.

qrdBas-b1102z.summary: The item assigned to Book 2 distinctions 43-44 is textually fragmentary. Folios 167v-168r are missing from the witness, and a further discontinuity at 169r leaves three topics only partly preserved. (1) The surviving end of a question on interior and exterior sin, close to d42: thought is in the will's power, given distinct (not merely habitual or universal) prior cognition of it. So sin can occur in thought alone through morose delectation, while delighting in evil as knowable is not sin. The will is a per se partial cause of the mental word, and circularity is avoided because objects cause through their representations. Speech and deed are sinful through the will's command and their deviation from their ends. Sin is divided five ways (effects, roots, branches, objects, precepts), and interior and exterior acts are one by order but formally two sins. (2) A fragment on the sin against the Holy Spirit (d43): it is called irremissible because it is in fact never or only rarely forgiven, not absolutely so. The closing replies confirm that it is a distinct sin though every mortal sin offends the whole Trinity, that Christ speaks of difficulty of remission, and that the 'sin unto death' is final impenitence. (3) A fuller article on the power of sinning (d44). Distinguishing power as principle, as real relation, and as relation of reason, Bassolis holds that the power of sinning, taken as the created will, is from God and good in its positive reality, while God causes neither the deformity of sin nor the merely potential relations. Against two other opinions, he holds that the will, as power of sinning, is intrinsic to created free choice and belongs to the image of the Trinity, while the relations to sinning only accompany it. Free choice in common abstracts from peccability, since God and the blessed (whose power to sin is never actualized) have freedom without sinning. The Book II commentary then ends with the printer's colophon (Paris, 1516).
claims: Thought is within the will's power, so sin can occur in thought alone through morose delectation.
The will is a per se partial cause of the mental word.
Interior and exterior acts form a unity of order but are formally two sins.
The sin against the Holy Spirit is irremissible only in a qualified sense: it is rarely or never forgiven in fact.
The power of sinning, taken as the created will, is from God and good in its positive reality; God does not cause the deformity of sin.
The will as power of sinning is intrinsic to created free choice, while relations to sinning merely accompany it; free choice in common abstracts from peccability.
